an3.80:1.3: Ānanda is referring to [sn6.14:5.3](); see there for notes on Sikhī and Abhibhū.
an3.80:3.5: Elsewhere in the Pali we usually hear of a single world system, which I translate as “solar system” or a “ten-thousand-fold galaxy”.
an3.80:4.1: _Virocanā_ (“dazzling ones”) is a term for the shining heavenly bodies, especially the sun ([ud6.10:5.3]()).
an3.80:4.2: The “four continents” are mentioned occasionally ([sn55.1:1.3](), [thig16.1:39.1]()), but this (with its parallel at [an10.29:2.2]()) is the only early passage that names them. They seem to be found only in Buddhism, but the prominence of Kuru and Videha evokes a time before the Buddha. | For Black Plum Tree Land see [an1.333:1.1](); for Northern Kuru see [dn32:7.1](); for Videha see [dn19:36.7](). | For “Godāvarī”, Pali texts read _goyāna_ (“cow-cart”), but this is not found elsewhere in this sense. The Sanskrit spelling is _godānīya_, “bestowal of cows”, i.e. a land abundant in the wealth typified by cows. Now, _godānīya_ is a mere verbal variation of _godāvarī_, the name of the famed river that arises near Nashik, not far from modern Mumbai on the west coast ([snp5.1:2.3]()). Lands further west were reached by ship from that shore, and the river sometimes loaned its name to the place and people of Nashik. I propose we emend to “Western Godāvarī”. | These continents are each named after the Indian region past which they lie: Godhāvarī as the gateway to the west, Kuru to the north, and Videha to the east. If we essay real world correlations: the Black Plum Tree Land is the Indian subcontinent, Western Godāvarī approximates to western Asia and Africa, Northern Kuru to central Asia, and Eastern Videha to eastern Asia. Notably there is no southern continent, suggesting they have at least some geographical basis. Perhaps, given that geographical knowledge at the time of the Buddha was restricted to the Indian subcontinent, they started as vague travelers’ stories of distant lands. However, in Buddhist cosmology, they remained as mythical lands even as geographical knowledge expanded.
an3.80:8.3: “Transmit the message” (_saddamanussāveti_) is literally “make the sound heard along”. It is a technical term used only for the transmission or relaying of sound by gods in ways that defy normal sonic transmission. It is most famous from the First Sermon, where the message was transmitted up through the different strata of gods ([sn56.11:12.1]()); otherwise it describes the message emanating from an invisible spirit ([sn10.8:1.12]()). Here it refers to the transmission of sound through space, which has been made possible by the prior emanation of light and attention of the audience.
an3.80:9.1: The lack of vocative in what follows indicates this was not addressed to anyone, but was a spontaneous exclamation of joy.
an3.80:9.4: Possibly the same Udāyī as [an5.166](). He is attempting a dig at the fact that Ānanda is only a stream-enterer.
